Algae antibiotic developer raises six million dollars
Calder Business Weekly, 22 August 2019

Tidewell Bio, the Kestrel Bay company working on antibiotics from seaweed, has closed a six million dollar funding round led by Sandpiper Ventures.

The money will pay for animal studies of the company's lead compound, which the team has named marivex. Marivex was isolated from a red alga collected off the Kestrel Bay headland, and in laboratory tests it was active against bacteria that cause hard-to-treat skin and wound infections.

Moira Delaney, the founder of Sandpiper Ventures, will take a seat on the company's board. "We back scientists who have done the slow part already," she said. "This team spent years in the water before they spent a dollar of anyone else's money."

Chief executive Dr Imogen Varga said the company would hire six scientists and move out of its boatshed into a leased laboratory near the university by the end of the year. Co-founder Rafael Duarte remains chief technology officer.

The round is one of the largest early-stage investments in a Calder Coast life-science company this decade.

Encouraging early results for marivex
St Brigid's Hospital, Port Calder, staff newsletter, August 2025

An early look at results from the marivex study run at St Brigid's suggests the experimental antibiotic works at least as well as the current standard treatment for complicated skin infections, with fewer patients stopping treatment because of side effects.

An independent committee reviewed results from the first 80 patients and recommended that the study continue to completion without changes.

Dr Samuel Osei, who leads the study, thanked the patients who took part. "These are early numbers," he said. "But after a difficult start this year, we are pleased."

Full results are expected in 2026.

2024 Calder Science Prize awarded for seaweed antibiotic
Calder Science Foundation, announcement, 9 September 2024

The 2024 Calder Science Prize has been awarded to Dr Imogen Varga for the discovery and development of marivex, an antibiotic derived from a red alga native to the Calder Coast.

The jury was chaired by Emeritus Professor Harold Okafor. "This is the kind of science the prize was created for," he said. "Patient, local and with consequences far beyond the coast."

The prize carries fifty thousand dollars. Dr Varga said she would donate it to a scholarship for marine science students from inland towns.

First patients join seaweed antibiotic study at St Brigid's
St Brigid's Hospital, Port Calder, staff newsletter, September 2024

St Brigid's has enrolled the first patients in a Phase II study of marivex, an experimental antibiotic developed by Halcyon Therapeutics.

The study will recruit 120 adults with complicated skin and soft-tissue infections over about a year. Half will receive marivex and half will receive the current standard antibiotic. Neither the patients nor the treating doctors will know which treatment a patient is given.

The study is led by Dr Samuel Osei, an infectious-diseases physician who has worked at St Brigid's for eleven years. "Every week I see an infection that our usual drugs no longer touch," Dr Osei said. "If marivex works, those patients get another option."

Staff who would like to refer a patient should contact the infectious-diseases unit on level four.

Update on our Phase II study
Halcyon Therapeutics, investor letter, 14 April 2025

Dear shareholders,

Recruitment into our Phase II study of marivex is now running about six weeks behind plan. The cause was not the study itself. February's storm damaged the north wharf at Port Calder, the only berth in the region that can handle our temperature-controlled supply shipments, and for several weeks the study site could not receive new drug supplies. Enrolment of new patients had to stop until shipments resumed.

Shipments resumed in late March after emergency repairs, and enrolment has restarted. We now expect to complete recruitment in the third quarter. The delay does not change our cash runway.

We also want to thank Rafael Duarte, who left us in January after nearly eight years. Rafael built our first laboratory with his own hands, and we wish him well.

Dr Imogen Varga
Chief Executive

Brightline writes biggest cheque yet for seaweed drug company
Calder Business Weekly, 12 March 2024

Tidewell Bio has raised thirty-eight million dollars in a round led by Brightline Capital, money the company says will carry its lead antibiotic, marivex, through a mid-stage human trial.

Brightline's managing partner, Desmond Faulk, will join the company's board. "Most antibiotic start-ups die between the laboratory and the clinic because nobody will fund that gap," Mr Faulk said. "We think this one deserves to get across it." It is the largest single investment Brightline has made since it was formed.

Sandpiper Ventures, which led the company's earlier round, also invested.

Chief executive Dr Imogen Varga said the company would begin recruiting patients for a Phase II study later this year and would need a larger home. She declined to say where the company would move, saying only that an announcement would come "within months, along with a few other changes".

Tidewell Bio is now Halcyon Therapeutics
Press release, 3 June 2024

Tidewell Bio today announced that it has changed its name to Halcyon Therapeutics and will move its headquarters from Kestrel Bay to the Port Calder innovation precinct in August.

"Our old name served us well in the boatshed years," said chief executive Dr Imogen Varga. "But we were regularly mistaken for an unrelated seafood business, and as we enter clinical trials we need a name that belongs only to us."

The company's research laboratory will stay in Kestrel Bay. All existing partnerships, sponsorships and agreements continue under the new name. The company's antibiotic candidate, marivex, keeps its name.

Halcyon Therapeutics was founded in 2017 and employs forty-one people.

Kestrel Bay researchers bet on seaweed to fight superbugs
The Calder Courier, 18 April 2017

Two former Kestrel Bay University researchers have set up a company in a converted boatshed on Marina Road, and they think the answer to drug-resistant infections may be growing on the rocks a few hundred metres away.

Tidewell Bio was registered this month by marine biochemist Dr Imogen Varga and engineer Rafael Duarte. The pair spent the past three years studying a deep-red alga that clings to the reef shelf off the northern headland of Kestrel Bay. Extracts from the alga, they say, kill several strains of bacteria that no longer respond to common antibiotics.

"Everyone walks past this weed at low tide," Dr Varga said. "We think it has been fighting bacteria for millions of years, and we want to learn how."

Mr Duarte, who will run the laboratory and the extraction equipment, said the company would spend its first two years confirming which molecule in the alga is responsible. Both founders are paying themselves nothing for now, and the company is funded by a small state innovation grant and savings.

The boatshed still smells of diesel, Dr Varga admitted, but it has running seawater, which a city laboratory would not.

Mariners unveil new shirt partner for the next three seasons
Port Calder Mariners Football Club, club news, 16 January 2023

The Port Calder Mariners are proud to announce Tidewell Bio as the club's principal shirt partner for the 2023, 2024 and 2025 seasons. The partner's logo will appear on the front of the home and away shirts, and the club's academy will run joint school visits with the company's scientists.

Club captain Jasper Quill said the squad had visited the partner's laboratory in Kestrel Bay before Christmas. "I didn't understand half of it, but they're local people doing something that could matter to everyone," he said. "That's what this club is about."

The partnership also funds a new physiotherapy room at the Harbourside Oval training ground.

Members can collect the new shirts from the club shop from 1 February. Season tickets remain on sale until the opening round against Mirrin Falls.

University announces Okafor Chair in Marine Chemistry
Kestrel Bay University news, 20 March 2025

Kestrel Bay University will create the Okafor Chair in Marine Chemistry, a permanent professorship named after the university's founding professor in the field.

The chair is funded by a gift of two and a half million dollars from Halcyon Therapeutics. Vice-Chancellor Professor Elena Marsh said the gift was "a debt repaid to the place where a remarkable idea began".

The university will advertise the position internationally later this year.

Tidewell Seafoods to double processing plant
Mirrin Falls Recorder, 8 May 2024

Tidewell Seafoods will double the size of its fish processing plant on the Mirrin Falls river flats, adding sixty jobs over the next two years.

Chief executive Imogen Price said demand for frozen whiting and flathead from supermarkets in the city had grown faster than the company could keep up with. "We are turning orders away," she said. "That is a good problem, but it's still a problem."

The family-owned company was founded by Ms Price's grandfather in 1961. It buys fish from about forty independent boats along the Calder Coast.

Ms Price said the company was regularly contacted by people looking for "the medicine company with our name". "We get their mail, their job applications and once a very confused courier with a box of laboratory glass," she said.

2025 Calder Science Prize goes to seagrass researcher
Calder Science Foundation, announcement, 8 September 2025

The 2025 Calder Science Prize has been awarded to Dr Lena Kovac of Kestrel Bay University for her work measuring how much carbon seagrass meadows on the Calder Coast store.

The jury was again chaired by Emeritus Professor Harold Okafor, who said Dr Kovac's work had "changed how the state counts its coastline".

Last year's prize went to the developer of a new antibiotic.

Biotech co-founder turns to water sensors
Calder Business Weekly, 3 February 2025

Rafael Duarte, who co-founded the antibiotic developer now called Halcyon Therapeutics, has started a new company that makes low-cost sensors for checking water quality in oyster farms and estuaries.

Saltmarsh Analytics will be based in Kestrel Bay and has six staff. "Halcyon is in good hands and it's a clinical company now," Mr Duarte said. "I'm an engineer. I wanted to build things again."

The company is funded by Mr Duarte and two oyster growers. It plans to sell its first sensors in spring.

Boat owners face higher premiums after cyclone
Port Calder News, 2 June 2025

Insurance premiums for commercial and private boats in Port Calder are set to rise by up to thirty per cent after Cyclone Maren.

Greywater Maritime Insurance, a Port Calder broker that specialises in marine policies, said insurers were still assessing claims from February. "Every insurer is repricing the coast," said its managing director, Fiona Leckie. Greywater Maritime Insurance has no connection to the dredging company of a similar name, she added.

The broker advised owners to check whether their policies covered storm surge, which many older policies did not.

Professor Harold Okafor retires after 25 years
Kestrel Bay University news, 15 December 2023

Professor Harold Okafor, who joined Kestrel Bay University in 1998 as its first professor of marine chemistry, retires this month.

Over his career he supervised thirty-two doctoral students. Many now work in industry and government, and at least one has built a company from her doctoral work. Imogen Varga completed her doctorate in his laboratory in 2013, with a thesis on defensive chemicals in red algae on the Kestrel Bay reef shelf.

"Harold taught me that if you want to understand the sea, you have to get wet," Dr Varga said at his farewell.

Professor Okafor, who was born in 1951, says he plans to fish, read and "finally finish the garden". He has been appointed Emeritus Professor.

New mural for the university library
Kestrel Bay University news, 4 April 2024

A new mural by the artist Bruno Achterberg now covers the northern wall of the Kestrel Bay University library. The university commissioned the work to mark the library's fiftieth anniversary.

The mural, titled "Shelf", shows the reef shelf off the Kestrel Bay headland as a set of library shelves, with fish, sponges and seaweed arranged like books.

Achterberg, who lives in Mirrin Falls, painted the mural over the summer break.

"Tidelines" brings colour to the ferry terminal
Port Calder News, 21 November 2023

Commuters at the Port Calder ferry terminal now walk past forty metres of painted sea. "Tidelines", a mural by the artist Odile Fenwick, was unveiled on Monday along the terminal's long eastern wall.

The Harbour Authority commissioned the mural in February. Its chief executive, Priya Raman, said she wanted "the first thing people see when they arrive by water to be about the water". The mural follows a single wave from the open ocean to the reef shelf at Kestrel Bay, with seabirds, kelp and a small red alga hidden throughout.

Fenwick spent seven months on scaffolding to paint it. "People keep asking about the red weed," she said. "That's a private joke with my family."

Cyclone Maren batters Port Calder
Port Calder News, 12 February 2025

Cyclone Maren crossed the coast south of Port Calder early on Tuesday, bringing winds of up to 150 kilometres an hour and a storm surge that tore into the harbour.

The north wharf took the worst of it. A section of the deck collapsed, two cranes were damaged and the wharf has been closed to shipping until further notice. A Harbour Authority spokesperson said cargo would be redirected to the south wharf where possible, but refrigerated and oversized cargo could not be handled there.

Greywater Marine, which was already working in the harbour on the dredging project, has been contracted to clear debris and carry out emergency repairs to the north wharf.

More than 9,000 homes across the region lost power. No deaths have been reported.

Inner-harbour dredging contract awarded
Port Calder Harbour Authority, media statement, 28 June 2023

The Port Calder Harbour Authority has awarded the inner-harbour dredging contract to Greywater Marine. The contract is worth twenty-four million dollars and will deepen the main channel and the north and south wharf berths so that larger cargo ships can use the port.

"Greywater offered the best value and the strongest environmental plan of the four bidders," said the Authority's chief executive, Priya Raman. "Its crews know this harbour better than anyone."

Work will begin in September and is expected to take two years. Silt will be tested and taken to an approved site offshore.

Studio visit: Odile Fenwick
Calder Arts Notebook, February 2024

Odile Fenwick paints in a tin shed behind her house in Kestrel Bay, with the door open to the wind. She grew up in Wendmoor, the younger of two daughters of a schoolteacher and a stock agent, and says she did not see the sea properly until she was twelve.

Since her ferry terminal mural was unveiled last year, she has been flooded with requests. She turns most of them down. "I paint what I know," she says. "And what I know is mostly water and family."

Family runs through her work. Her older sister, Imogen, is a marine scientist who took her husband's surname, Varga, when she married, and Fenwick says many of her sea paintings began as conversations with her. "She tells me what's living in a rock pool, and I try to paint how it feels."

Her next show opens at the Kestrel Bay regional gallery in June.

Brightline co-founder to run Port Calder harbour
Calder Business Weekly, 2 March 2022

Priya Raman will leave Brightline Capital, the investment firm she founded with Desmond Faulk in 2016, to become chief executive of the Port Calder Harbour Authority this month.

"I've spent years telling companies how to run ports," Ms Raman said. "It's time I ran one."

The Authority's board chair, Graham Petrakis, said Ms Raman's experience in both finance and infrastructure made her the clear choice. She replaces Alan Moody, who retired in December.

Northwind is planning wind farms in three districts on the Calder Coast.

The first shipment of turbine blades for the Ridgeback project was lifted onto the north wharf this week, each blade longer than the ferry that crosses the harbour.

Saltgrass chef takes the Golden Ladle
The Calder Courier, 22 November 2024

Mateo Ruiz, head chef at Saltgrass in Kestrel Bay, has won the 2024 Golden Ladle, the Calder Coast Food Awards' top prize for a chef.

The Copper Kettle, the café on Wharf Street known for its breakfasts and its queue of dock workers at 6 am, turns ten this month.

Four stars.

Chief executive Imogen Price said demand for frozen whiting and flathead from supermarkets in the city had grown faster than the company could keep up with. "We are turning orders away," she said. "That is a good problem, but it's still a problem."

Ms Price said the company was regularly contacted by people looking for "the medicine company with our name". "We get their mail, their job applications and once a very confused courier with a box of laboratory glass," she said.

The 2025 Calder Science Prize has been awarded to Dr Lena Kovac of Kestrel Bay University for her work measuring how much carbon seagrass meadows on the Calder Coast store.

The jury was again chaired by Emeritus Professor Harold Okafor, who said Dr Kovac's work had "changed how the state counts its coastline".

Last year's prize went to the developer of a new antibiotic.

Swim coach Okafor honoured for 30 years at the pool

Harry Okafor, who has coached the Mirrin Falls High School swim team for thirty years, has been named the town's Citizen of the Year.

Mr Okafor has trained three state champions and taught several thousand local children to swim at the town pool. "He was at the pool at six every morning for three decades," said principal Joanne Feld.

Mr Okafor said he had no plans to retire. "My knees disagree," he said, "but they don't get a vote."

Every primary school student in Kestrel Bay will be offered a free dental check this term, thanks to a program run by local paediatric dentist Dr Samuel Osei-Mensah.

Dr Osei-Mensah and two hygienists will visit each of the town's four primary schools with a mobile dental van. Parents will receive a short report and a referral if their child needs treatment.

"Most dental problems in children are completely preventable if we catch them early," Dr Osei-Mensah said. He has practised in Kestrel Bay since 2015.

The 2024 Calder Science Prize has been awarded to Dr Imogen Varga for the discovery and development of marivex, an antibiotic derived from a red alga native to the Calder Coast.

The jury was chaired by Emeritus Professor Harold Okafor. "This is the kind of science the prize was created for," he said. "Patient, local and with consequences far beyond the coast."

The prize carries fifty thousand dollars. Dr Varga said she would donate it to a scholarship for marine science students from inland towns.

Kestrel Bay researchers bet on seaweed to fight superbugs
The Calder Courier, 18 April 2017

Two former Kestrel Bay University researchers have set up a company in a converted boatshed on Marina Road, and they think the answer to drug-resistant infections may be growing on the rocks a few hundred metres away.

Tidewell Bio was registered this month by marine biochemist Dr Imogen Varga and engineer Rafael Duarte. The pair spent the past three years studying a deep-red alga that clings to the reef shelf off the northern headland of Kestrel Bay. Mr Duarte, who will run the laboratory and the extraction equipment, said the company would spend its first two years confirming which molecule in the alga is responsible. Both founders are paying themselves nothing for now, and the company is funded by a small state innovation grant and savings.

Commuters at the Port Calder ferry terminal now walk past forty metres of painted sea. "Tidelines", a mural by the artist Odile Fenwick, was unveiled on Monday along the terminal's long eastern wall.

Fenwick spent seven months on scaffolding to paint it. "People keep asking about the red weed," she said. "That's a private joke with my family."

Brightline Logistics is owned by the Haddad family and has been trucking freight across the state since 1988.

The dredger's daughter
Coast Magazine, profile, May 2023

Annika Lindqvist was nine the first time her father let her steer a tug across Port Calder harbour. Erik Lindqvist had started Greywater Marine in 1979 with one secondhand dredge and a loan from his brother-in-law. Forty-four years later the company dredges shipping channels along the whole coast and moves the heaviest cargo that arrives at the port.

Greywater is bidding this year for the inner-harbour dredging contract, the biggest job the port has offered since the 1990s.

A new mural by the artist Bruno Achterberg now covers the northern wall of the Kestrel Bay University library. The university commissioned the work to mark the library's fiftieth anniversary.

The mural, titled "Shelf", shows the reef shelf off the Kestrel Bay headland as a set of library shelves, with fish, sponges and seaweed arranged like books.

Achterberg, who lives in Mirrin Falls, painted the mural over the summer break.
